cells.tense: You're tending it right now — two hands on the thing that feeds everyone, and neither hand is clenched.
cells.verb: tending what you've been given to carry, carefully and on purpose
cells.place: in what gets handed down and shared — the recipes, the songs, the way your people do things
cells.ask: offer one thing you made or keep to someone who'd carry it further, and let what they do with it be theirs — release comes easily when the work feels finished, and that ease is the point to let yourself have
cells.core:
You're tending it right now — two hands on the thing that feeds everyone, and neither hand is clenched. That's rarer than it sounds. What you keep going is not just yours; it's the version of it that other people will still have when you're not the one holding it. And you're not forcing it to grow faster than it will. You're feeding it at the pace it can actually take.

You know the difference between care and control, which most tenders don't until something breaks. Two demands pull at you — the ones who need it now and the length of time it takes — and you're holding both without picking a favorite. That holding is the work. Nobody clocks it, and it's the work.
cells.sheetLine: You care for what's been passed to you without gripping it.

cells.tense: You're already bracing for a harvest that hasn't been planted yet — planning the table before the field is even turned.
cells.verb: tending past what's actually growing, forcing the pace of something that has its own time
cells.place: in the traditions and shared things you're protecting — except you're protecting a future version of them nobody asked for
cells.ask: let one thing you're tending get to where it's going without your hand on it — vision comes back when what you've already lived gets digested first, so let a day pass that you don't steer
cells.core:
You're already bracing for a harvest that hasn't been planted yet — planning the table before the field is even turned. The care is real. The timing isn't. You're spending today's tending on tomorrow's problem, and the thing you're protecting can feel your grip even when you're being gentle.

Somewhere ahead there's a version of this where it's all held, all safe, all cared for — and you're living in that version instead of this one. What's suffering is the actual thing, right here, which doesn't need the future. It needs you now, unbraced.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the pace of something that has its own.

cells.tense: You set it down a while back, and you're still standing at the spot where you put it.
cells.verb: having stopped tending what you used to care for — the hands are still, but the grief isn't
cells.place: in the shared things — the practices and traditions you used to keep alive
cells.ask: start one small thing back up, badly, just for yourself — strength comes back from continuing to hope, from the shining that shows up when what you tended finally ripens, so give one seed a little water this week and don't ask it to prove anything
cells.core:
You set it down a while back, and you're still standing at the spot where you put it. Something happened — a room where your care landed wrong, or a time when tending cost more than you had — and the tending stopped. The thing you care about didn't go anywhere. The offering did.

You can still name what you love about it. You can still tell what it should be. That knowing is the caretaker in you, intact. What's gone quiet is the reaching. Not the care itself — the arm.
cells.sheetLine: The care is still there; the tending stopped.

cells.tense: You're already keeping something alive across time — it moves through how you do things, what you pass on, what you refuse to let go — and you'd never put your name on the keeping.
cells.verb: tending and passing on, without ever claiming you're the one tending
cells.place: in the shared meaning of things — except you describe it as just how it is, or just what your people do
cells.ask: say out loud to one person that something you keep going is yours to keep — things get released when they're finished, and they get finished when they're seen, so let one thing you've been carrying be witnessed as carried by you
cells.core:
You're already keeping something alive across time — it moves through how you do things, what you pass on, what you refuse to let go — and you'd never put your name on the keeping. You call it just the way things are done, or just what you grew up with, as if the thing were tending itself.

The keeping is running. The claim on it isn't. People around you can feel the care in how you handle what matters; you can't feel it in yourself because you never stopped to sign it. Sign it. Not for credit — because unnamed care is exhausting in a way that named care isn't.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it alive, and you talk like it keeps itself.
